questions.question: Which command creates a new Django project named mysite?
questions.explanation: startproject creates the project (manage.py + the settings package). startapp creates an application inside an existing project.

questions.question: Which commands display the installed Django version?
questions.explanation: Both run the same django-admin program. 'pip show django' would also work, but none of the other spellings exist.

questions.question: Which statements about python manage.py runserver are true?
options: It starts a lightweight server meant for development only
By default it listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000/
It is the recommended server for production
It creates every database table on startup
It compiles the project into an executable
It installs missing packages from requirements.txt
questions.explanation: runserver is a development tool. Tables are created by migrate, and production uses a WSGI/ASGI server.

questions.question: Which statements about the files created by startproject are true?
options: manage.py is a management script you run but do not edit
asgi.py is where views are written
questions.explanation: urls.py holds routes, models live in each app's models.py, and __init__.py only marks the folder as a Python package.

questions.question: What are wsgi.py and asgi.py used for?
options: They are entry points for WSGI / ASGI compatible web servers
questions.explanation: A production server (gunicorn, uvicorn, ...) imports the application object exposed by one of these files.

questions.question: Why create a virtual environment before running pip install Django?
options: To isolate the project's dependencies from the system Python
To pin a Django version per project without affecting other projects
Because Django refuses to install globally
To make the development server faster
Because manage.py only runs inside a venv
To get a database for free
questions.explanation: Same reasoning as Lesson 3: each project gets its own isolated, reproducible set of packages.

questions.question: Which command adds an application named polls to an existing project?
questions.explanation: startapp creates the polls/ folder with models.py, views.py, admin.py, apps.py, tests.py and migrations/.

questions.question: Which statements about Django projects and applications are true?
options: A project can contain several applications
An application is meant to be reusable in other projects
An application can never be reused outside its project
A project contains exactly one application
An app is active as soon as its folder exists
django.contrib.admin is a project, not an app
questions.explanation: An app must also be added to INSTALLED_APPS to be active. admin, auth, sessions... are themselves apps.

questions.question: Which statements about this view are true?
options: It receives an HttpRequest object as first argument
It must return an HttpResponse (or a subclass)
A view must always be a class
The view should print() the HTML
The request parameter can be omitted
Returning a plain str works: Django converts it
questions.explanation: Returning a plain string makes Django raise an error: a view must return an HttpResponse object.

questions.question: Where can you see the applications already used by a new project?
options: In the INSTALLED_APPS list of settings.py
questions.explanation: INSTALLED_APPS already contains admin, auth, contenttypes, sessions, messages and staticfiles.

questions.question: Which INSTALLED_APPS entries correctly activate the polls application?
questions.explanation: Both work: 'polls' lets Django find the default AppConfig, 'polls.apps.PollsConfig' names it explicitly (the course's form).

questions.question: With these two files, which URL displays views.index?
questions.code:
# mysite/urls.py
path("polls/", include("polls.urls")),

# polls/urls.py
path("", views.index, name="index"),
questions.explanation: The project prefix 'polls/' is concatenated with the app route '' (the root of the application).

questions.question: Which statements about include() are true?
options: It delegates every URL starting with a prefix to another URLconf
It lets each application keep its own urls.py
It copies the views' code into urls.py
questions.explanation: include('polls.urls') strips the matched prefix and passes the rest of the URL to polls/urls.py.

questions.question: What does the name argument of path() allow?
options: Referring to the URL by name, with {% url %} in templates or reverse() in Python
Nothing: it is required for the page to load
questions.explanation: name is optional. With it, changing the URL later does not break links built with {% url 'name' %}.

questions.question: Which URL displays views.hello?
questions.code:
# mysite/urls.py
path("polls/", include("polls.urls")),

# polls/urls.py
path("hello", views.hello, name="hello"),
questions.explanation: Project prefix + app route: 'polls/' + 'hello'.

questions.question: The route is path("hello", views.hello). What happens when you open /polls/hello/ (with a final slash)?
options: A 404 error: the route has no final slash, so it does not match
questions.explanation: APPEND_SLASH only adds a missing slash (it redirects /hello to /hello/ when that route exists). It never removes one.

questions.question: Why should path("", include("theme_material_kit.urls")) be placed last in urlpatterns?
options: Django tries patterns in order and keeps the first match, so a catch-all placed first would hide our routes
Because include() only works at the end
Because the admin must always be first
Because the order changes the speed of migrations
questions.explanation: Lowest priority = end of the list: only URLs not handled by our own apps fall through to the theme.

questions.question: What is the correct order to create or update a table?
options: Edit models.py, run makemigrations, run migrate
Run migrate, run makemigrations, edit models.py
Run makemigrations, edit models.py, run migrate
Edit models.py, run migrate, run makemigrations
Edit models.py and restart the server: tables update automatically
questions.explanation: 1) define the models, 2) makemigrations records the change, 3) migrate applies it to the database.

questions.question: Which statements about python manage.py makemigrations polls are true?
options: It writes migration files describing the changes in the models
It does not modify the database
It applies the changes to the database
questions.explanation: makemigrations creates polls/migrations/0001_initial.py. Only migrate touches the database.

questions.question: What does python manage.py sqlmigrate polls 0001 do?
options: It prints the SQL that migration 0001 would run, without executing it
questions.explanation: Useful to check what will happen to the database. For the polls models it prints two CREATE TABLE and one CREATE INDEX.

questions.question: Which statements about the default database are true?
options: Data is stored in an SQLite file named db.sqlite3
It can be changed in the DATABASES setting of settings.py
The data is stored in models.py
Data is lost each time the server restarts
PostgreSQL must be installed before running migrate
questions.explanation: SQLite needs no server, which suits development. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle... can be configured in DATABASES.

questions.question: Why is the migration mechanism useful?
options: It upgrades the production database by replaying the changes made in development
It keeps a history of schema changes, like commits in Git
It copies development data to production
It backs up the database automatically
It removes the need to write models
questions.explanation: Migrations track the structure (tables, columns), not the data.

questions.question: On a brand new project with no model written yet, why does python manage.py migrate already create tables?
options: The pre-installed applications (auth, admin, sessions...) ship their own migrations
Django creates one table per URL
migrate fills the database with sample data
db.sqlite3 is copied from a template
questions.explanation: Those apps already defined their models and migration files: we only need to apply them.

questions.question: You add a field to a model but forget makemigrations and migrate. What happens?
options: The table has no such column, so queries on that model fail with an error such as 'no such column'
Django adds the column when the server restarts
The field is silently ignored and everything works
migrate alone detects the change and alters the table
questions.explanation: migrate only applies existing migration files. Without makemigrations there is nothing new to apply.

questions.question: Which statements about this relation are true?
questions.code:
class Choice(models.Model):
    question = models.ForeignKey(Question, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    choice_text = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    votes = models.IntegerField(default=0)
options: Each Choice is linked to one Question
A Question can have several Choices
Each Question has exactly one Choice
A Choice can belong to several Questions
ForeignKey creates a new table for questions
ForeignKey copies the question text into Choice
questions.explanation: A ForeignKey is a many-to-one relation: it stores question_id in the choice table.

questions.question: What does on_delete=models.CASCADE mean on Choice.question?
options: Deleting a Question also deletes its Choices
Deleting a Choice also deletes its Question
A Question cannot be deleted while it has choices
The choices are kept with question set to NULL
The choices are moved to another question
It has no effect with SQLite
questions.explanation: PROTECT would forbid the deletion and SET_NULL would keep the choices with an empty question.

questions.question: Which statements about these fields are true?
options: "date published" is a human readable name for the field
A DateTimeField stores a date and a time
"date published" is the default value of the field
pub_date is set to the current time automatically
question_text accepts any number of characters
default=0 makes votes mandatory with no default
questions.explanation: The first positional argument of a field is its verbose name, used for example in the admin. max_length=200 limits question_text.

questions.question: The Question model declares no primary key. What does Django do?
options: It adds an auto incremented primary key named id
Nothing: every model must declare its own id
It uses question_text as primary key
It creates the id only after the first query
It resets id to 1 on each save
questions.explanation: That is why q.id displays 1 after the first q.save().

questions.question: Which statements about defining __str__ in a model are true?
options: It changes how objects are displayed, for example in a QuerySet or in the admin
It does not require a new migration
It adds a column to the table
It changes the value of question_text
It is required for save() to work
questions.explanation: Without it the shell shows <Question: Question object (1)>; with it, <Question: What's up?>. It is pure Python, the schema is unchanged.

questions.question: With USE_TZ = True (the default), how are datetimes such as pub_date handled?
options: They are stored in UTC and converted to TIME_ZONE when displayed in templates
They are stored in the server's local time
They are converted to the browser's time zone by Django
questions.explanation: timezone.now() returns an aware UTC datetime. A raw f-string in a view shows the UTC value, while a template displays the local TIME_ZONE time.

questions.question: What does python manage.py shell open?
options: An interactive Python prompt connected to the project, where the models can be imported
A bash terminal inside the database
questions.explanation: Each command is evaluated and its result displayed, which is ideal to experiment with the models.

questions.question: The question table is empty. What does Question.objects.all() display in the shell?
options: An error: the table is empty
questions.explanation: objects.all() returns a QuerySet, not a list, even when it is empty.

questions.question: The table is empty. Which statements are true right after this line, before q.save()?
options: The object only exists in memory: nothing is in the database yet
questions.explanation: Instantiating a model does not touch the database. save() runs the INSERT and fills q.id.

questions.question: q is already saved with id 1. What does the second save() do?
options: It updates the existing row, which keeps id 1
It inserts a new row with id 2
It deletes the row and recreates it with a new id
questions.explanation: save() runs an UPDATE when the object already has a primary key, an INSERT otherwise.

questions.question: Which statements about q.choice_set are true?
options: Django creates choice_set automatically because Choice has a ForeignKey to Question
q.choice_set.create(...) creates a Choice linked to q and saves it
choice_set must be declared in the Question class
q.choice_set.count() counts every choice in the database
The choice is only saved after a later q.save()
questions.explanation: The reverse relation is named <model in lowercase>_set. count() only counts the choices of that question.

questions.question: What does Pakiman.objects.filter(level__gt=5) return?
options: The Pakiman whose level is strictly greater than 5
The Pakiman whose level is greater than or equal to 5
The Pakiman whose level is lower than 5
An error: gt is not a field
questions.explanation: Lookups are written field__lookup: gt, gte, lt, lte, exact, contains, icontains...

questions.question: Which expressions return every Pakiman with a level of at least 5?
questions.explanation: get() returns a single object and fails if there are several. level >= 5 is a Python comparison, not a lookup. gt excludes 5.

questions.question: No question has id 99. What does Question.objects.get(id=99) do?
questions.explanation: filter() would return an empty QuerySet instead. In a view, get_object_or_404() turns this case into a 404 page.

questions.question: Where does Django look for an application's templates by default?
options: In a templates/ folder inside the application
In the static/ folder of the project
questions.explanation: APP_DIRS = True in TEMPLATES makes Django search each installed app's templates/ folder.

questions.question: Which statements about render(request, "questions.html", context) are true?
options: It fills the template with the context and returns an HttpResponse
Each key of the context dict becomes a variable in the template
render() saves the template in the database
render() sends the page by email
questions.explanation: context = {"questions": ...} lets the template use {{ questions }} and {% for question in questions %}.

questions.question: In the Django template language, what are {{ ... }} and {% ... %} used for?
options: {{ }} displays a value, {% %} runs a tag such as for or if
{{ }} runs a tag, {% %} displays a value
{{ }} is a comment, {% %} displays a value
questions.explanation: Comments are written {# ... #}.

questions.question: Why is question.choice_set.all written without parentheses in the template?
options: The template language calls methods automatically and does not accept parentheses
It is a mistake: it should be .all()
all is an attribute, not a method
It displays the method object instead of calling it
Parentheses are only forbidden inside for loops
questions.explanation: Method calls with arguments are impossible in a template: prepare that data in the view.

questions.question: Which statements about the {% for %} tag are true?
options: A {% for %} block must be closed with {% endfor %}
{% empty %} inside the loop is rendered when the list is empty
The loop closes automatically at the end of the line
{% end %} closes any kind of block
Python's for ... else is used in templates
Indentation defines the body of the loop
questions.explanation: Indentation means nothing in a template: the end of each block is explicit.

questions.question: The view receives p = "hi". Which statements are true?
options: With {{ p }} in a template, the page shows the literal text hi, because variables are escaped
Concatenated into an f-string inside HttpResponse, the same value would be interpreted as HTML
With {{ p }} the page shows hi in bold
Django raises an error when a parameter contains HTML
Escaping only happens in the admin
questions.explanation: Auto-escaping protects templates against HTML / JavaScript injection. Hand-built HTML must call django.utils.html.escape().

questions.question: Why use a template instead of building the HTML in the view?
options: It separates the processing (view) from the display (template)
Templates run faster than Python code
Templates store the data in the database
questions.explanation: This split is the MVC pattern, called MVT in Django: Model, View (the controller), Template.

questions.question: What do {% extends "ynav/base.html" %} and {% block content %} do?
options: The page reuses the layout of base.html and only fills in its content block
They import Python code into the template
They concatenate two HTML files one after the other
They only work in the admin
questions.explanation: Template inheritance avoids repeating the <head>, the navbar and the CSS links on every page.

questions.question: The URL is /ynav/query?p=hello. Which expressions give "hello" in the view?
questions.explanation: request.GET is a dictionary-like object holding the query string. request.POST holds the body of a submitted form.

questions.question: The URL is /ynav/query, without any parameter. Which statements are true?
options: request.GET["p"] raises an error (a KeyError subclass)
questions.explanation: Prefer .get(), possibly with a default value: request.GET.get("p", "").

questions.question: The URL is /ynav/query/range?min=1&max=5. What does request.GET.get("min") return?
questions.explanation: Query parameters are always strings: convert them with int() and handle the ValueError.

questions.question: Which URL passes first_name=John and last_name=Doe?
questions.explanation: ? starts the query string, & separates the parameters.

questions.question: low = 1 and high = 5. Which expression gives the numbers 1 2 3 4 5?
questions.explanation: range() excludes its end bound.

questions.question: Which statements about NameForm are true?
options: name is a form field, rendered as a text input
NameForm creates a table in the database
forms.CharField and models.CharField are the same class
The form must be added to INSTALLED_APPS
questions.explanation: A forms.Form describes fields and their validation only: there is no table behind it.

questions.question: Which statements about this view are true?
options: is_valid() runs the validation and fills cleaned_data
On a GET request, an empty form is displayed
cleaned_data can be read before calling is_valid()
is_valid() saves the form in the database
The form should be sent with GET to avoid CSRF checks
questions.explanation: request.POST holds the submitted fields. cleaned_data only exists after is_valid().

questions.question: What happens when a POST form does not contain {% csrf_token %}?
options: Django rejects the request with a 403 Forbidden error
Django converts the request to GET
The server crashes with a 500 error
questions.explanation: The CSRF token proves the form was produced by our site and not by a malicious page.

questions.question: Why does pakiman_add redirect after a successful POST instead of rendering a page?
options: So that refreshing the page does not submit the form a second time
Because render() cannot be used after a POST
Because a POST view cannot return status 200
questions.explanation: This is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern: the browser ends on a GET page, safe to reload.

questions.question: Which statements about a ModelForm such as PakimanForm are true?
options: Its fields are generated from the model listed in Meta
form.save() inserts the object into the database
Its fields must be declared twice
It only works in the admin
questions.explanation: is_valid() also checks the model validators, for example MinValueValidator(1) on level.

questions.question: Which command creates an account that can log into /admin?
questions.explanation: A superuser has every permission, like root on Linux.

questions.question: Which code makes both Question and Choice editable in the admin?
options: Adding Question and Choice to INSTALLED_APPS
class Meta: admin = True in each model
questions.explanation: register() accepts a single model or a list of models.

questions.question: Which statements about the admin application are true?
options: It provides a CRUD web interface on the registered tables
The Users and Groups tables come from the auth application
It can be used without logging in
It must be installed separately with pip
questions.explanation: django.contrib.admin is installed by default, reachable at /admin/ and protected by a login page.

questions.question: Which steps are needed to activate theme_material_kit?
options: Add "theme_material_kit" to INSTALLED_APPS, before our own apps
Run python manage.py migrate, since a new app was added
Copy its files into our templates/ folder
Put its URLs first in urlpatterns
questions.explanation: The package is installed with pip (via requirements.txt), and its URLs go last: path("", include("theme_material_kit.urls")).

questions.question: Which forms are provided by django.contrib.auth.forms?
questions.explanation: UserCreationForm is the registration form, AuthenticationForm the login form used by LoginView.

questions.question: What is a custom filter such as {{ field|add_class:"input" }} useful for?
options: Adding a CSS class (e.g. Bulma) to the widget Django generates for a form field
Saving the field in the database
questions.explanation: Custom template tags and filters live in <app>/templatetags/ and are loaded with {% load <module> %}.

questions.question: What does this list comprehension produce?
questions.explanation: Each element is incremented, the list keeps 4 elements. (The course text says [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]: that is a typo.)

questions.question: What does datetime.datetime.now().strftime('%H:%M') return at 9:05 am?
questions.explanation: %H = hour (24h), %M = minutes. Lowercase %m is the month.

questions.question: Why use triple quotes in HttpResponse("""<html> ... </html>""")?
options: To write a string over several lines
To make the string a comment
questions.explanation: A triple-quoted string keeps its line breaks.

questions.question: n = 5. What is the last element of this list?
questions.code: rows = [(i, n * i) for i in range(1, 11)]
questions.explanation: range(1, 11) goes from 1 to 10 included, the template then prints '5 x 10 = 50'.

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: "".join() concatenates the strings with an empty separator.

questions.question: Which settings are part of the deployment checklist?
options: Keep SECRET_KEY out of the code, e.g. in an environment variable
Keep DEBUG = True to see the errors
questions.explanation: ALLOWED_HOSTS must list the site's domain names when DEBUG is False. django-environ helps read settings from a .env file.
